name: Calendly
whyPeoplePay: Calendly sells the end of the scheduling email thread, and it works because the other person never has to sign up for anything. What you are renting is a link that stays alive, a page that renders correctly on a stranger's phone, and connectors into Google, Outlook, Zoom and Salesforce that keep working after those vendors change something. The free tier deliberately stops at one event type, which is exactly where a working habit starts costing money.

plans.name: Free
plans.note: One event type, one calendar connection. Advertised as always free.

plans.name: Standard
plans.note: $10 per seat per month on annual billing, which is the figure the pricing page shows by default under a Save 16% label.

plans.name: Teams
plans.note: $16 per seat per month on annual billing, shown under a Save 20% label. This is the tier that adds round robin and shared team pages.

plans.name: Enterprise
plans.note: The pricing page states it starts at $15,000 a year and sends you to sales for a number.

pricing.note: The pricing page renders its annual-billed figures by default: we read $10 and $16 per seat per month with Save 16% and Save 20% labels beside them, and Enterprise starting at $15k a year. We record the monthly-billed rates because that is what a month-to-month subscriber actually pays, and those two numbers ($12 and $20) come from the page's own discount percentages rather than from a toggle we were able to click, corroborated against third-party pricing summaries on the same day. Confidence is medium until someone re-reads the page with monthly billing selected.

ranked.rationale: The only one here that is the same product rather than a smaller cousin: event types with buffers and minimum notice, a public booking page, calendar sync, webhooks and an API. The costs are honest ones. It is the heaviest install in this category, wanting 4 GB and a PostgreSQL, its first boot genuinely looks broken for ten minutes, and the teams and routing features that justify Calendly's Teams tier sit behind a commercial licence key you will not have. Take it if you want your own booking domain and one person's calendar; look elsewhere if you came for round robin.

evaluatedNotTested.name: Rallly
evaluatedNotTested.note: Actively developed, AGPL-3.0, releasing steadily through 2026. It answers the other scheduling question: not "book a slot on my calendar" but "which of these times works for all eight of us", which is Doodle's job rather than Calendly's. Lighter to run than Cal.com and a genuinely better fit if group polls are what you actually do, but it will not give you a personal booking page.

evaluatedNotTested.name: Easy!Appointments
evaluatedNotTested.note: GPL-3.0, PHP and MySQL, still maintained. Built for businesses booking customers into staff schedules, with services, providers and working plans. It has since earned its own page in this catalog as the Acuity Scheduling answer, where its business-front-desk install is written up in full; on this page Cal.com keeps the top spot for personal scheduling links.
